chunks: Routing the buck input capacitor. The question: How should you route the input capacitor?
A buck converter turns a higher steady (DC) voltage into a lower one by switching it on and off very fast.
Each switch pulls a sharp pulse of current from a small input capacitor next to the chip.
The wiring to that capacitor acts like a tiny inductor, and fast current changes make voltage across it. So you put the capacitor right against the chip's input and ground pins.
Think of a water pipe with a valve at the end. Slam the valve shut and the moving water can't stop at once, so you get a pressure spike. The longer the pipe, the bigger the bang.
The pulsed current is the water, and long wiring is the long pipe. A small tank right beside the valve absorbs the surge.
The picture covers only the spike; real circuits also ring.
Left, both capacitor pads touch short copper stubs from the VIN and PGND pins and the ground via is at the capacitor, so the red loop encloses a tiny area.
Right, the capacitor sits away from the pins on long traces and the return goes through a via, so the loop is many times larger and has more inductance.
Buck converter: a circuit with two switches and a coil that steps a DC voltage down. Input capacitor: a small part that stores a little charge and supplies the current pulses.
Inductance: how strongly a wire or loop resists changes in current. Longer loops have more. 1 nanohenries is a billionth of a henry.
Hot loop: the path the pulses take: capacitor, upper switch, lower switch, back. VIN and PGND pins: the chip's input-voltage pin and its power-ground pin.
The voltage across an inductance is V equals L times (how fast the current changes). Say the current jumps 5 amps in 3 nanoseconds.
A tight layout has about 3 nanohenries, so the spike is 3 nanohenries times 5 amps / 3 nanoseconds = 5 volts .
With the capacitor far away the loop is 10 nanohenries, and the spike is about 17 volts , a lot on a 12 volts input. That is the whole idea.
"The input capacitor closes the hot loop with the two switches, so I put a small ceramic, 0.

1 to 1 microfarads in 0402 or 0603, right against the VIN and power-ground pins on the same layer, with short wide copper, no vias in between, and the ground via at the capacitor pad over a solid plane.
A larger ceramic goes next to it and a bulk capacitor farther away. The reason is inductance: 3 nanohenries with 5 amps in 3 nanoseconds is 5 volts of overshoot."
